title: Igulim and yosher: the dream that surrounds everything, and the deed that rules it
overview:
The *Kav* goes down from the *reshimu*, circles, goes down and circles again: the *igulim* are one line. In them the highest surrounds all and is best, and the innermost is lowest; in *yosher* it is the other way around. To see why, the chapter looks at the *ratzon kadum*, the original will. It is revealed compared to the *ratzon hamuchlat*, but still hidden and for oneself, like the stirring to have things your own way before you know it means a house, and it already holds every detail, down to the bathroom drapes. In the *Zohar*'s words it is *Atika d'Atikin*, and in the *Keser* of *Adam Kadmon*, *Atika Stima'a*; the delight already in *chachma*, in *Atzilus*, is *Atika Kadisha*.

In the circles every cause surrounds its effect, and the effect never reaches it, as a kid's reasons never capture why he wants a bike. When the will comes to be done in actual fact, it reverses: will hides in intellect, intellect in *middos*, *middos* in the deed, and the *sof maaseh* becomes king. *Igulim* are *teshuva*, *yosher* good deeds. Of the Essence above the *Kav* nothing can be said: the *tzimtzum* is a jump, not a line.

terms.gloss: circles: the sefiros one inside the other, where the outermost, the will, is the main thing and everything inside is a token of it
the straight line: the sefiros enclothed one in the lower one in the shape of a person, where the deed is on the outside and on top
the original (not merely first) will: the origin of every detail, revealed compared to the ratzon hamuchlat but still hidden and for oneself
the final deed: in the circles the flimsiest daydream and the innermost; in yosher the top thing that everything has to fit
the Atik of all Atiks: the ratzon kadum as the inner pleasure behind all pleasure, the source of the pleasures in things outside oneself
the will of all wills: the same ratzon kadum, called by its will, since the taanug is the will inside the will
the hidden Atik: the Keser of Adam Kadmon, where the will is already associated with a thought; covered, but meant to be revealed
the most hidden of all hidden: the beginning of the Kav, which even the thought of Adam Kadmon cannot grasp
the holy Atik: the delight already in chachma, in a particular form; Atik Yomin and Arich Anpin of Atzilus
the bribe: the will makes the intellect biased, so it finds reasons to fit
the short line: one little point of the essence that stands for all of it, the jump from the reshimu to the ratzon kadum
the impression left after the tzimtzum: every possible limited thing, His choices of style without seeing Him in them; still infinite

sections.title: Circles and the straight line: one line that goes down and circles
sections.summary: The chapter sets out to explain the details of the *Kav* as it is in *igulim* (circles). The beginning of the *Kav* goes down a little, circles, goes down and circles again, so that the circles are really one line; in the circles the highest is the best and the innermost the lowest, and in *yosher* (the straight line) it is the other way around.

phrases.en: Now we have to start to understand

phrases.he: בפרטי ענין הקו כמו שהוא בבחינת עגולים כו'.
phrases.en: We have to understand how the *Kav* is already *igulim*

blocks.text:
We just finished explaining the *igulim* (circles), and the difference between the *ratzon hamuchlat* (the absolute will) and the *ratzon murkav* (the composite will). **Now we have to start to understand**, "because until now we didn't understand anything."

**We have to understand how the Kav is already igulim.** Really we were supposed to explain *yosher* (the straight line) as well, but we do not really explain *yosher* until the next chapter. Here he starts to tell you a little bit about it, but not so much. So now we have to understand the details.

We explained the general idea of what *igulim* means. It is like the *ratzon* (will) for a house: there is the general *ratzon*, and inside it, it includes all the particular *ratzonos*; it divides into a bunch of particular desires, and each one is like a circle. Why a circle? Because it includes everything inside of it equally. It is like one point that includes everything, like making the context: the whole context defines everything.

phrases.he: והנה תחלה יש להקדים בבחינת ראשית הקו הזה
phrases.en: So first we have to explain about the *reshis hakav*

phrases.he: שבא בבחינת אור פנימי ואחר כך מתעגל ונמשך בבחינת אור פנימי וחוזר ומתעגל כו'
phrases.en: first it comes down; the very first *hiyuli Kav* comes down from the *reshimu*, then it circles, and then it goes down and then it circles

blocks.text: **So first we have to explain about the reshis hakav** (the beginning of the line), before we get into the *igulim*. As it says, **first it comes down**: the very first *hiyuli* (raw, general) *Kav* comes down from the *reshimu* (the impression left after the *tzimtzum*); **then it circles, and then it goes down and then it circles.**

blocks.title: Drawing it without lifting the pen
blocks.text: You might picture a bunch of concentric circles with a line going through them, but that is not really the way it goes. Really the circles are made of the line. It is as if you drew that same image without picking up your pen. First you go down, let's say, a centimeter; then you draw a circle until you come back to the point where you were; then you draw another line going down another centimeter and draw another circle; and another, and another, concentric circles, smaller and smaller. It is really one line.

phrases.en: and it explains in *Etz Chaim*

phrases.he: שבבחינת עשר ספירות דעגולים, העליון מכולם משובח מכולם והפנימי מכולם גרוע כו',
phrases.en: the best one is on the outside, and the worst one, the lowest *sefira*, is on the inside

phrases.he: ובבחינת עשר ספירות דיושר להיפך, העליון גרוע והפנימי משובח כו'.

blocks.text:
**And it explains in Etz Chaim** that in the ten *sefiros* of *igulim* the highest is the most praised and the innermost is the lowest, and in the ten *sefiros* of *yosher* it is the opposite.

What is the difference between *igulim* and *yosher*? In *igulim*, *Keser* (crown) is on the outside and *Malchus* (kingship) is on the inside: **the best one is on the outside, and the worst one, the lowest sefira, is on the inside.** In *yosher*, each *sefira* is *mislabesh* (enclothed) in the one under it. The *Keser* goes into the *Chabad*, the *Chabad* goes into the *middos* (emotional attributes), and the *middos* go into thought, speech and action. So the outermost one is the *Malchus*, thought, speech and action. Inside the action are thought and speech, inside them the *middos*, inside them the intellect, inside that the *ratzon*, and then the *taanug* (delight). If you drew it, that is the difference: whether you draw *Keser* on the outside and *Malchus* on the inside, or *Keser* on the inside and *Malchus* on the outside.
Before we talk about circles and things, we have to understand what *igulim* and *yosher* are. What does a circle mean, and what does a line mean? What are we talking about?

sections.title: The ratzon kadum: a hidden first will for yourself that already holds every detail
sections.summary: The *ratzon kadum* (the original will) is revealed compared to the *ratzon hamuchlat*, but it is still hidden, a will for oneself, like the inner stirring to have things your own way before you know it means a house. It is the origin of every detail down to the last blade of grass, and the last deed, the end of the seventh millennium, was first in thought.

phrases.en: the explanation of these matters, these things

phrases.he: הנה ידוע שבחינת רצון קדום זה,
phrases.en: that this first *ratzon*, the *ratzon* for the house in the *mashal*

phrases.he: הגם שלגבי בחינת רצון הפשוט המוחלט בעצמות
phrases.en: even though compared to the *ratzon hamuchlat*
it's already called like a particular revealed *ratzon*
But the truth is, it's really still hidden
it's not revealed at all

phrases.he: כי אינו רק השפעת והמשכת רצון הפשוט של חפץ חסד שהוחלט בעצמות מכבר, כך יהיה בפועל ממש
phrases.en: All you know is that you want your *ratzon hamuchlat* to be revealed *b'poel mamash*

blocks.text: **The explanation of these matters**: it is known **that this first ratzon**, the *ratzon* for the house in the *mashal* (analogy), **even though compared to the ratzon hamuchlat it's already called like a particular revealed ratzon**: you went from having just a taste to actually having a *ratzon* for a house, so it is already a revealed desire that you want a house. **But the truth is, it's really still hidden; it's not revealed at all.**

What this first *ratzon* means is that you do not yet know what you want. **All you know is that you want your ratzon hamuchlat to be revealed b'poel mamash** (in actual fact). That is what that first *ratzon* is. In other words, you do not want a house yet; in a way you do not even want a home yet. A house you do not want until *Beriya*, *Yetzira* and *Asiya*, and even a home you do not really want yet, because you did not even reach the *yosher* of *Adam Kadmon*.

blocks.title: Your parents are cramping your style
blocks.text: All you have is an inner stirring. People have this at a certain age: they want different things, they want to be independent, they want their own space. You do not know what it is yet; you just feel that you do not like the way things are, and you want things to be the way you like them. You feel cramped; your parents are cramping your style. You are at home and you want to leave the house, and your mother tells you that you have to wear a sweater because it is cold, and wash your hands, and all these things are in your hair, and you feel they are cramping your style. So you just have this *ratzon* to have things the way you want them to be.

But before that, you do not even know that this means having your own house and your own job and your own life, and you certainly did not figure out what kind of house, or where, or what kind of job. It is just this *ratzon*, which you have had ever since you were a little kid, to have something independent that expresses yourself, the way you want it to be. It is just an inner desire to be yourself.

"I mean, it doesn't sound right, 'to be yourself,' 'cause you can't not be yourself. It's ridiculous: 'I want to be myself.'" What do people mean when they say they want to be themselves, or find themselves, or understand themselves? What they really mean is that they want to figure out how to get the world to express themselves, how to make it fit with them.

blocks.title: Getting the world to play your song
blocks.text:
It is like a guy who is trying to play an instrument: he wants to learn how to get the world to play his song. He really knows what he wants to play, even if he does not realize it, because he does not think in terms of music. You can have a *ratzon* for a song in your head already, and that is like having a *ratzon hamuchlat*: certain things sound good to you. But you do not know what song it is until you bring it out into the instrument. That is the *hiyuli* that has to come out.

So really this *ratzon kadum* is still hidden. You still do not know what you want; you know, but not in a tangible way.

phrases.he: ומיד שעולה במחשבה זאת שיהיה הכל,
phrases.en: as soon as it comes up in your thought, I want to do everything that was in my *ratzon hamuchlat*
that's called the first *machshava* and *ratzon*, or the original
which includes everything that's inside of it
all the particular desires inside of it
like we said about the *mashal* of the *ratzon* for a house

blocks.text: **As soon as it comes up in your thought**, "I want to do everything that was in my *ratzon hamuchlat*," **that's called the first machshava and ratzon, or the original**: the *machshava kduma* and *ratzon kadum*.

blocks.title: A father and a firstborn
blocks.text: *Kadum* really means original; it does not mean first. In English, original means that it is the origin of everything else, and everything else is just a branch from it. First just means that it happens to be the first one. It is like the difference between a father to his children and a firstborn. A father you call *kodem*: he precedes them, he is their origin. The firstborn just happens to be first.

So this is the original *ratzon*, **which includes everything that's inside of it, all the particular desires inside of it, like we said about the mashal of the ratzon for a house.** As soon as you say, "I want a house," or "I want a home," automatically all the other *ratzonos* are included in that. So this is not a first *ratzon* that just happens to be first. The only reason you want the kitchen sink is that you want a house. It is all included, and it is predicated on your having the general *ratzon* for the house. They are defined by it and included in its definition: your definition of a house includes all those things.

phrases.he: אם כן עדיין רצון קדום זה הכל בעצמו
phrases.en: So, if so, this first *ratzon* is still totally within G-d Himself
it's not revealed yet outside, in anything separate
nevertheless, from it comes everything
afterwards
And this is what it says

phrases.he: כי הוא אמר, במחשבה הקדומה, ויהי כו'
phrases.en: that G-d said, and it was

blocks.text:
**So, if so, this first ratzon is still totally within G-d Himself.** In a person, when his *ratzon* for the home first comes up, he is not thinking of anything outside of himself. He is thinking about something in himself: that he wants to feel a certain way, to express a certain style, a certain taste. He does not want something outside himself. So **it's not revealed yet outside, in anything separate.**

**Nevertheless, from it comes everything afterwards**, because everything is just the expression of that *ratzon*.

**And this is what it says**, "For He said," with the *machshava kduma*, "and it was": **that G-d said, and it was.** Whenever it says *amar* (said), by the way, it really means *machshava* (thought). Even when it means speech, it means that you are saying what is on your mind, just saying what you are thinking.

blocks.title: A proclamation and a chat with friends
blocks.text: When you make an official proclamation, you are not just saying what is on your mind; you are making an official statement. The focus there is that it is *dibur* (speech), that you are saying it. When you are sitting and talking with your friends casually, the focus is not on what you are saying but on what you are thinking. You say, "Yeah, you know what I mean," because you are not focusing on the words and that they have to be exact. Any time you focus on the thought behind it, as opposed to the words, it is called *amira*; when you focus on the words, it is called *dibur*.

So where it says "For He said, and it was," it means that He revealed Himself in a way of *machshava*, or at least the *machshava* of *dibur*: a level focused on thought, a *gilui* (revelation) of thought, and there are different levels of that. Here he is talking about the *ratzon kadum*, which is called the first, original thought. So **G-d said**: in other words, He said to Himself. He figured out, He decided, how He wanted the world to be, **and it was**: it all came to be according to that. As soon as G-d told Himself, "I want a world, I want a *dira b'tachtonim* (a dwelling below)," everything else just follows from that automatically. Everything else is just part of doing that one thing, making the *dira b'tachtonim*.

phrases.en: And this is called the life of all the worlds
from the beginning of *Adam Kadmon*
until the heel of *Adam Kadmon*
all the way down to the end of *Asiya*

phrases.he: והיינו כל היצור לא נכחד כו'
phrases.en: all of the formed things are not missing from You

phrases.he: שאין פרט היותר אחרון שלא קדם להיות ברצון ובמחשבה זו
phrases.en: There is nothing, not even the smallest detail, that escaped G-d's first *ratzon* and *machshava*; it was all there

blocks.text:
**And this is called the life of all the worlds**: this is what gives life to all the worlds. The motivation behind everything is this one point, **from the beginning of Adam Kadmon** (which will be explained next chapter) **until the heel of Adam Kadmon**, since *Adam Kadmon* is a general *partzuf* (stature) that goes all the way to the end of all the worlds, **all the way down to the end of Asiya**, as will be explained later.

This is what we say, "I think," in the *davenen* (prayers) of Rosh Hashana, in *Zichronos*: **all of the formed things are not missing from You.** What does that mean?

**There is nothing, not even the smallest detail, that escaped G-d's first ratzon and machshava; it was all there.** The last, smallest little detail was there, the last hair on your head. Did G-d really care, did He know and think about how many hairs are going to be on my head? Yes. That is why we say that everything is *hashgacha pratis* (individual Divine providence), even the way a leaf blows in the tree and the grass blows. G-d knows exactly how it is going to happen, exactly how many times it is going to blow back and forth. And not only does He know: it is *noge'a* (relevant) to the entire purpose. For the completion of the *dira b'tachtonim* and *Moshiach*, the original *ratzon* that G-d wants, it has to be exactly like that.

blocks.title: The bathroom drapes
blocks.text: You say, "What? Why does that make a difference? That's ridiculous." Well, think about when you want a house. The whole thing of wanting a house is that you want it exactly the way you want it. Say you have the resources and money is no object. You build the house and do everything, down to the little nitty-gritty things, the bathroom drapes and the decorations, the little things you care about. If one of those little things is off, you did not really get what you wanted. You are living there and you are comfortable, but the original *ratzon* you do not really have: that thing that it is your house, your space. That is why, if you are renting and the landlord will not let you change your windows, it is not a real house, because you cannot just do what you want with it.

blocks.title: The bathroom drapes
blocks.text: It is such a little *prat* (detail), but if you want it different and you cannot do it the way you want it, it takes away the whole thing. It could be a good house, but it loses the quality that this is all your house. The bathroom drapes are just as important as the general structure, and if you are missing even one little *prat*, the whole thing loses out. "It's all or nothing deal."

So why does the grass have to blow exactly that way? Because G-d wanted it to be a certain way, for whatever reason. That is what made Him feel good, and if it is not like that, even one little thing, then the whole thing is stupid: who needs it? "If a grass won't blow 7,296 times, what's it all worth?" What is the point of making the world? It would all have been so perfect, but that one blade of grass would not be right, and it would ruin everything. So it was all included in this first *ratzon kadum*.

blocks.title: Going out for pizza
blocks.text: Say, "Shmuel, what do you want to do tonight?" "Let's go out for pizza." That has all the details. That is the *ratzon* to open the door. How do you know you want to open the door? Where am I going to get it? You say, "It's all there, don't worry, we got you covered."

phrases.en: On the contrary

phrases.he: סוף מעשה, כמו בסוף אלף הז', עלה במחשבה קדומה זו תחלה
phrases.en: the last thing was really the first in thought

blocks.text: **On the contrary**: the final deed, as at the end of the seventh millennium, came up first in this *machshava kduma*. The final *ratzon* to eat the pizza, to chew on it and swallow, that was the first thought. "So, don't worry, you have the *ratzon* to chew." In the same way, G-d's main *ratzon* was for the end of the seventh millennium, with all the little details of how it is going to be then. So we are getting closer and closer to the main *ratzon*.

You say, "Ah, it's just little details," but in a way these are the main things that G-d wanted. As we go through history, in a way it becomes less, and in a way it becomes more. It started off with people like Adam and Avraham, the big pushers and movers. They were general people, and their stories were meaningful to all mankind and represent everybody. "Yeah, what about us? The other day I had a story happen to me; why doesn't it get recorded for all times?" In a way they have an advantage, because they are more general, earlier up in the *hishtalshelus* (the chain of descent).

But the main *ratzon* was really for when you go on *mivtzaim* (outreach campaigns) and put *tefillin* on some guy, or when you learn some *maamar* (discourse). **The last thing was really the first in thought.** When it comes to your *ratzon hamuchlat*, the actual wall structure of your house is the least important. Most people do not build the house themselves from scratch; they buy a house, decorate it themselves and put in their own furniture. The main *gilui* of the *ratzon hamuchlat* is not in the main things, which are just functional. It is in the little things, where there is no practical reason and it is just about how you like it. That is the biggest *gilui* of your *ratzon hamuchlat*.

In the same way, the biggest *gilui* of G-d's *ratzon hamuchlat* is in "the stupid little things": the way G-d wants the world set up for *Moshiach*, that He wants it *davka* (precisely) this way and *davka* that way. "He could have done it in another way." "Yeah, but He likes it this way." Even now: why are trees green? Why aren't the leaves brown and the trunks green, or a totally different color? Or why couldn't you hear the difference between the leaves and the trunk? It gets harder to appreciate as you go higher up, but there are certain things where it is just, "Why does it have to be like that?" Why does there have to be a bird-dropping spider? "Nobody knows why." And there is room to say more about it.

sections.title: In the language of the Zohar: Atika d'Atikin, Atika Stima'a and Atika Kadisha
sections.summary: A parenthesis puts the *ratzon kadum* into the *Zohar*'s terms. In the *ratzon* there is a *taanug*, and they are one: as the source of all the pleasures and wills to come, in the *Kav* after the *tzimtzum*, it is *Atika d'Atikin*, the pleasure of all pleasures; enclothed in the *Keser* of *Adam Kadmon*, already associated with a thought, it is *Atika Stima'a*, hidden but meant to be revealed; and as the pleasure already in a particular form, in *Atzilus*, it is *Atika Kadisha*.

phrases.en: in the words of the *Zohar*
the *ratzon kadum* is called the *Atik* of all *Atiks*, the inner pleasure behind all pleasure
or the hidden *Atik*

phrases.he: והוא בחינת רעוא דכל רעווין עילאין
phrases.en: This is also the *ratzon* of all upper *ratzonos*, the inner *ratzon*
which is revealed on the forehead of *Atika Kadisha*
because the *ratzon* inside the *ratzon* is the *taanug*
And they're really one thing

blocks.text: **In the words of the Zohar**: "Now we're going to do this kabbalistic parentheses to put everything in context for you. Since you're used to learning things in Zoharatic terminology, we're going to now help you translate it into your mother tongue, all right? Ready for this?"

In the *Zohar*'s language, **the ratzon kadum is called the Atik of all Atiks, the inner pleasure behind all pleasure** (*Atika d'Atikin*), **or the hidden Atik** (*Atika Stima'a*). There is a difference between the two, but he is not getting into that now; at the end of the parenthesis he explains it.

**This is also the ratzon of all upper ratzonos, the inner ratzon** (*ra'ava d'chol ra'avin*). So it is both the inner *taanug* and the inner *ratzon*, **which is revealed on the forehead of Atika Kadisha**: of the *taanug* revealed in something particular. That is the Zoharic terminology.

Why is it called both *Atika d'Atikin* and *ra'ava d'chol ra'avin*? **Because the ratzon inside the ratzon is the taanug. And they're really one thing**, so you can call it the *ratzon*, the *ratzon kadum* or the *taanug*; "you can call them whatever you want to call it."

phrases.he: וברצון הפשוט ההיולי שבחפץ חסד ההיולי (הנזכר לעיל באות יוד ואות יא) היה כלול בו התענוג
phrases.en: Even in the *hiyuli ratzon pashut* there was enclosed the *hiyuli taanug pashut*

phrases.he: הפשוט שבעצמות שנקרא שעשועי המלך בעצמותו כו'

phrases.en: in each of the three levels there's a *ratzon* and there's also the *taanug*
until it comes to a *prat*
that I'm going to be king

phrases.he: שזה בחינת מלכות דאין סוף שלפני הצמצום
phrases.en: which is the *Malchus d'Ein Sof* before the *tzimtzum*, which is the *ratzon hamuchlat* for our world

phrases.he: הכל בחינת שעשועי המלך בעצמו בטהירו עילאה
phrases.en: Those are all G-d's essential *taanug* in Himself

blocks.text:
In the simple, *hiyuli* will of the *hiyuli chafetz chesed* (the desire for kindness), explained in chapters 10 and 11, was included the simple delight of the Essence: **even in the hiyuli ratzon pashut there was enclosed the hiyuli taanug pashut.** And **in each of the three levels there's a ratzon and there's also the taanug, until it comes to a prat**, *Ana Emloch*, **that I'm going to be king, which is the Malchus d'Ein Sof before the tzimtzum, which is the ratzon hamuchlat for our world.**

**Those are all G-d's essential taanug in Himself.** Before, we talked about it more from the side of the *ratzon*, but there is also the side of the *taanug*: the pleasure G-d has in Himself.

phrases.en: but once you talk about *Atika d'Atikin*
which is the source of all pleasures, meaning pleasures you have in things separate from yourself
or the *ratzon* of all *ratzonos*
that's in the *Kav* that's after the *tzimtzum*
which is like one general *ratzon* or one general *taanug*, that you want to express yourself
that are going to come out *b'gilui*

blocks.text:
**But once you talk about Atika d'Atikin, which is the source of all pleasures, meaning pleasures you have in things separate from yourself, or the ratzon of all ratzonos, that's in the Kav that's after the tzimtzum.** It includes many wills and delights, **which is like one general ratzon or one general taanug, that you want to express yourself.**

So this is the intermediary between enjoying everything outside of you and enjoying yourself. Before it, it is all an enjoyment or a *ratzon* for yourself; after it, it is an enjoyment and a *ratzon* in things outside yourself. The intermediary is the *ratzon kadum*, in which you are expressing your *ratzon hamuchlat*. It is the source of all the desires and pleasures **that are going to come out b'gilui** (in revelation). That is why it is called *Atika d'Atikin*, the pleasure of all pleasures, and *ra'ava d'chol ra'avin*, the *ratzon* of all *ratzonos*.

blocks.title: Interviewing G-d
blocks.text: Say they are going to interview G-d: "Well, G-d, if You were going to make a world, how would You like it? Would You like being king of a universe?" And He says, "Yeah, I would really love being king of a universe, and I would want it to be like this and like that." G-d was sitting around daydreaming about what it would be like, but He did not actually want to do it.

Right then He was busy, "you know, playing with His train set." It's not *kavod* (dignified)? Playing chess? "Why G-d has to be like this sophisticated guy? He could be playing a little kid, why not?" That is not *kavod* in this *hishtalshelus*, because here He is the King, but then He was doing a different *hishtalshelus*. In this *hishtalshelus* G-d decided to reveal Himself in big things, in a dignified way, like a king; in another *hishtalshelus* He could do little things. "See, that's the best thing: G-d doesn't have any parents to tell Him what to do. They can't tell Him not to play with the trains, it's not *kavod*."

It is like association: when you learn a language, before you are actually thinking, you just know that this idea is associated with that sound. That is a *stima* thing.

So it is still hidden; only He thought **that He wants to actually have it: to have the revealed ratzon and taanug for the sefiros of Atzilus, and the revealed ratzon and taanug for Beriya and for Yetzira and Asiya also.**

blocks.text:
**Atika Kadisha, though, is the taanug that is in the chachma already**: a delight in something particular, already coming in a particular form. It is *Atik Yomin* and *Arich Anpin* of *Atzilus*, **the taanug and the ratzon of Atzilus**; **that's already a revealed ratzon.**

In other words, the original *ratzon*, called *Atika d'Atikin*, is the inner delight of yourself. Once it goes through *Adam Kadmon*, it becomes associated with a certain form, and then you get the delight that it should be *davka* in this form, because once you chose it, it is going to reveal you. That is the *taanug* and *ratzon* of *Atzilus*, called *Atika Kadisha*: holy, but already connected. **Like we'll explain everything in detail.**

So what did we explain so far? That even the *ratzon kadum*, which is the first *gilui* after the *Kav*, is still a hidden thing, still only for yourself. The *igulim* that come out until you get to *yosher* are all still for yourself; you have not thought about the world yet. All it means is that you are thinking that you want to come out into the world. It is ready to come out, because you already know that you want to reveal a certain thing and you want it in the world, but you have not yet figured out what that means. So it is still hidden. It is like the *ratzon* for a home before it becomes a *ratzon* for a house: you do not want a building yet, you just want to feel at home. It is still hidden, as far as not knowing yet what that means.

Sometimes people have these desires and do not know what they are. This happens a lot with people, especially Jewish people, "but even *goyim* also": they do not feel they are using their potential, they feel their life is empty, they are missing something and do not know what it is. They know how they want to feel, fulfilled, but they do not know what will give it to them, because the *ratzon* is still *b'helem* (hidden). They really know what they want, but until they figure out what it is, it can motivate them to try all kinds of weird things.

sections.title: Circles: each cause surrounds its effect, and the effect never reaches it
sections.summary: The ten *sefiros* of *igulim* are a wheel inside a wheel: every cause surrounds its effect, and the effect reaches it only from far away, as the reasons a kid makes up never capture why he wants a bike. Each circle starts as one undivided point, a bias, down to the *sof maaseh*, the final deed, which in the circles is the flimsiest and innermost; so too the *ratzon kadum* is ten circles, from the will for a *dira b'tachtonim* to the will for this exact world.

phrases.he: והנה בחינת עשר ספירות דעגולים זה תחת זה הוא כידוע,
phrases.en: the ten *sefiros* of *igulim*, one under the other
that every cause surrounds its effect
And the effect does not grasp, it doesn't reach its cause

like a wheel inside of a wheel

blocks.text: Now, **the ten sefiros of igulim, one under the other**: what does it mean that they are like ten spheres, a circle inside of a circle? As is known, **every cause surrounds its effect. And the effect does not grasp, it doesn't reach its cause**, its source, except **only in a very far away, very far from it, like a wheel inside of a wheel.** That is the *mashal*.

blocks.title: A wheel inside a wheel
blocks.text: The *mashal* of a wheel inside a wheel is that there is the inner source, the real thing you want, like the inner desire with the house; and then there is the lower thing that comes out from it, the way you are going to get it. But that will never really fully give you the thing you want. That really stays higher.

The quote is talking about Ezekiel's vision of the Divine chariot: he said that the *Ofanim* (a class of angels) look like a wheel inside of a wheel, with eyes all over them. That is the quote, but what we mean is concentric circles. The *mashal* is a wheel inside a wheel, a circle inside a circle.

blocks.title: Ripples in a pond
blocks.text: Concentric circles means a big circle, and inside it a smaller circle, all around the same center point, like ripples in a pond. Except that here it comes from the outside going in: first the outer circle, then the inner one, and the inner one, and the inner one. It is not like dropping a pebble in a pond, where it starts from the middle and goes out. But the truth is that even there, the biggest one goes out first, and inside of it come smaller and smaller ones. The first one starts off and gets bigger and bigger, and while it is getting bigger, smaller and smaller ones come inside it, and they all keep getting bigger; it keeps filling up with more and more.

And the truth is that this is the way the *hishtalshelus* of the *igulim* goes in the Ramak's *hishtalshelus*, where he is talking about it from the *reshimu*: there it starts from the middle and comes out like that. But we are talking about the Arizal's *hishtalshelus*, once it is already set up and the light is just going through it. So it comes from the top of the circle and goes in. That is the *mashal*: a circle inside a circle.

blocks.text: **Like the reason and the intellect for the ratzon, which is called its effect: it's impossible for it to be close to its source, its cause, which is the desire**, because there is no reason for a *ratzon* at all, **as is known.**

blocks.title: A kid who wants a bike
blocks.text: What are we talking about? A *mashal* of a person who wants something. Let's say a kid wants a bike. That is it, *nekuda* (period), as they say in Hebrew: he wants a bike, that's the point. At this level there is no reason, nothing; he wants it because he wants it. Once he decides he wants it, that causes him to make up all kinds of reasons why he should want it, to have excuses to tell his parents: "Oh, I can get to school faster, and it's healthy." Those reasons are being invented because of his *ratzon*; they are not making his *ratzon*. So his *ratzon* is the cause and they are the effect, a derivative of his *ratzon*.

blocks.title: A kid who wants a bike
blocks.text: Not only that: they do not quite capture the *ratzon*, so that is not the real reason he wants it. Tell him, "Oh, well, you don't need the bike to get to school, you can walk." "Wait, but I need to be there on time." "Also you can run. That way you get the exercise, and you get there on time. We'll jog there every day."

blocks.title: Helping shlep the couch
blocks.text: You see this a lot: people want something but do not want to say directly what they want, for whatever reason, so they give some side reason, to make it look like a rule, when really there is no rule, just what they want. Or they do not want to put the burden on themselves. "Oh, can you help me *shlep* my couch?" "Oh, I really would love to, but..." and some reason why they can't. At the end of the day they just don't want to, so they look for an excuse: "I have to do this, I have to do that." The advantage of saying a reason is that you take it off yourself: "It's not that I don't want to; something else is making me not able to."

blocks.title: Helping shlep the couch
blocks.text: But as soon as you do that, you make yourself susceptible to being put in a corner where you have to do it, because they can disprove your reason. "Oh, it's so perfect, I'll have somebody take care of the thing you had to do, and you can help me." "Oh, no, now look what I got myself into." Because the reason never really captures the *ratzon*; that is not really why.

blocks.title: A belief and its proofs
blocks.text:
The same with a debate, with a belief. Say people believe the Rebbe is *Moshiach*. "Well, why do you believe?" "Oh, this *sicha* (talk), this Rambam, this whatever." It does not mean it is not true. But the fact is that they believe it because they believe it, not because of these proofs. So if you disprove those things, they are not going to say, "All right, you're right, never mind." They will just find another proof, because the intellect comes from the *ratzon*, not the other way around.

That is going from *chachma* to *bina*: the belief makes up a proof. The *igul* (circle) of the *chachma* forces the *igul* of the *bina* to justify it, to prove it, but the proofs do not really capture the *chachma*. And the inner *ratzon* is for the Rebbe: they want the Rebbe to be *Moshiach*.

blocks.text: **Nevertheless, the chachma is coming from the ratzon.** And **the circle of chachma is also just a nekuda** (a point). **It's also without a recognizable division into ten**, because it is just like a bias. The fact that your *ratzon* makes the *chachma* be a certain way does not mean you have a particular *chachma*. It is the essence of the *chachma*: your *sechel* (intellect) is biased to lean in a certain direction, so whenever you come to a particular piece of reasoning, it will find something that fits.

blocks.title: A bias toward kindness
blocks.text: Let's say you have a *ratzon* toward *chesed* (kindness). That will make your intellect lean toward *chesed*, so you will be liberal-minded. Whether it is just toward your son, that you always look at him favorably, or in general, that you are liberal or conservative, politically or in anything. That is just a bias, an intellectual leaning, not a particular reasoning yet. In each case you will look for what you think will fit the view you want: you want things to turn out in a way of *chesed*, so you look for reasoning and a worldview that fit with that. Your *sechel* just leans that way. And yet the *sechel* will never really capture the *ratzon*; it is just a way to express the *ratzon* and get it to come out.

**This is like a bribe** (*shochad*): **the bribe makes you find the reason for the ratzon.** Because a person bribed you to make the court case go a certain way, you are biased to look at things in a certain way. You do not yet have a particular reasoning for why he should be innocent, but now you will always look at things with that bias.

**And even though this reason also includes ten sefiros, ratzon and sechel and middos**, a whole world of coming up with a reason and proving it, a whole thing to itself, it comes as a general thing: **right now you didn't develop and reveal all those pratim** (details); **right now it's just the point, the bias.**

blocks.text: **And so too the bina doesn't reach the chachma.** The proofs you bring to substantiate your claim, your view, are the *bina*; the claim or the view or the belief is the *chachma*; and they do not meet up. The proofs do not really prove it, and they will not really be able to change it either.
You see this more openly in alternative things: pseudo-sciences, New Age spirituality and cultish things. There is very little reasoning there; they bring one little proof and pile everything on it.

blocks.text: **And so too with each emotion, one after the other**: then it comes out that a certain thing is good and that you should like it, and so on through all the *middos*, **until it comes to sof maaseh** (the final action), **which is the last thing.** In a way it is the most fake and the most flimsy.

First of all, it is not an actual thing even. It is a total daydream, dreaming about things being a certain way, very fake; it is not really going to happen, and it is never really going to give you what you want. By the time you get down to action, you are not going to be able to get your inner desire, to be rich, or to have a house, even a home, to express your taste. It is such little things that in a way it does not capture what you want at all. It is such a limited self-expression of it.

blocks.title: A kid in a bakery with two bucks
blocks.text: That is why kids who go into a bakery or a store have trouble deciding what to buy. In your imagination you have so many things you want, so many things you can imagine, and all you have is two bucks. Even if you have enough money for any one thing, you can only walk away with one thing, and there are so many things there. The same in life: you can only do one thing, and it has to express all your emotions, all your taste and choices, your whole worldview and your whole inner desire, "and you know, it's like nothing."

**And all this is all in the desire for himself, which includes everything, till the final action.** Even the last *igul* is not all the *pratim* of how he is going to do it. It is just the bias, the *nekuda*, that he wants to do things a certain way, that he wants to do this: "Oh, I decide, I'm doing this." He has not figured out the *pratim* of how he is going to do it, **which is the innermost thing of everything.**

blocks.text: So too the hidden will, surrounded by all the other *igulim*. The biggest thing is the inner *ratzon*, whatever it is you want: let's say you want the house, the home. That makes a *chachma*, a certain picture. Then you make a *bina* to justify and explain it, to make distinctions: what kinds of things will make it closer to what you want and what kinds will make it farther. Once you divide it into parts, you can have *middos*.

blocks.question: Why can't you have middos from a chachma?
blocks.text: Because in *chachma* it is all or nothing. It either is or it is not, so you do not know how to react to something: how can you like it, like it more, like it less? Once you have *middos* from *bina*, you recognize that there are a bunch of parts, so you can be excited that it is getting closer.

You like this a little more, that a little less; you have to work on it, and slowly build it to the way you want. The *middos* are the way you react, change things and measure things out. If you are making a house, you have to decide how big to make your kitchen and the other rooms: the *middos*, even the physical dimensions, come from an understanding in *bina* of the picture in *chachma* of what you want in *Keser*.

You want to express your taste. Once you make a picture of what kind of thing expresses your taste, you can figure out all its parts, start drawing plans and figure out the details. Those details come out in the *middos*, and the *middos* come out in the *sof maaseh*, where you actually do something about it: you buy a house, or whatever.

You could design more than one house that would fit your *middos*, and you pick a certain one: "No, that's it, I want this one." "Why do you want this one?" "I want that one." That is also like a *nekuda*: you just make up your mind, and now that one is going to express everything, your inner *ratzon*. So it is the innermost thing. It is built on everything else and exists only within the context of everything else: the reason you want this *sof maaseh*, this house, is that it follows these *middos*, and you only care about those *middos* because they are within this *bina*, within this *chachma*.

blocks.title: Dressing in style
blocks.text: Say a person wants to dress in style. They want their clothes to have certain shapes and colors, which are like *middos*, so they buy a certain thing. Why that thing? Because it has certain characteristics, which are *middos*. Why do they care about those characteristics? Because in *bina* they associate them with being in style. The *chachma* is the picture they have of what it means to be in style, whatever picture they have, different groups and different things. And the inner *ratzon* is the desire to be in style, or to express themselves, depending how far in you want to go. So this thing exists only within the context of all the others around it. That is why it is called the *pnimi* (innermost): everything else surrounds it.

**This is the ratzon hane'elam, which is called the ratzon kadum, the source of all the ratzonos, and it includes ten sefiros.** In the same way, **so too the first ratzon that G-d had for the whole world is like this**: one general circle that includes all ten things in it, **in a way of a circle inside of a circle, until the circle of the sof maaseh.**

First there is the *ratzon* for a *dira b'tachtonim*, the most general. Then there is the *ratzon* that it should be in a certain form, the inner thing of *Atzilus*; then that the form should be associated with certain things; then certain *middos*; until a certain *sof maaseh*, the final *igul*: that G-d wants this world exactly the way it is. Because on the level of the *middos* you could still have infinite worlds that would meet those specifications.

And **the first circle that includes everything** is the *ratzon kadum*. Everything exists only within its context. The only reason G-d wants everything, at least the way He set up the *hishtalshelus*, is that it is part of this *ratzon* for a *dira b'tachtonim*. That is the main thing: everything exists only to be part of a *dira b'tachtonim*, "that's it." Nothing has meaning without it, and nothing alone ever reaches it. So the *gilui* in *Atzilus* does not really express that thing properly. He chose that it should go through that, but it does not fully capture it.

blocks.title: Giving flowers
blocks.text: You have to read between the lines; nothing captures it. You have to be able to appreciate, like giving flowers: that does not express anything, it is such a little thing. That is the point: the *etzem* (essence) stays as a *makif* (encompassing light) over it, like the thought, but it does not come into any *kli* (vessel). You see it from the context, that you are using it to express that thing, but it does not really do it properly. It is just a sign, a token.

blocks.title: The strings of the tallis
blocks.text: That is the idea of *tzitzis*. The *tallis* represents some big *makif* that goes around everything, and to express it to the next level you have to have strings that come out, which stand for making some token representation of it.

**Until the circle of the sof maaseh**, which is the *ratzon* for the final deed: **this is the ratzon for sof maaseh, that Hashem wanted to actually do everything that He wanted, to actually make the world.** And **the first circle that includes everything** is the *ratzon kadum* mentioned above.

That is the way it works with the *igulim*. First is the *ratzon kadum*, the original desire for the *dira b'tachtonim*, the seventh millennium. Then it goes all the way down, from the general desire for a *dira b'tachtonim* to the *ratzon* for the exact form of how the world is going to be, down to every last hair on your head. Then, once that picture of the world was decided, the whole of history and all of that, G-d decided He was going to do it *b'poel mamash*. That is the last circle.

sections.title: Yosher: once you decide to do it, the order turns over and the deed is on top
sections.summary: When the will for oneself comes to be done in actual fact, everything reverses: the *ratzon* hides in the intellect, the intellect in the *middos*, and the *middos* in the deed, until the *sof maaseh*, which in the circles was a daydream, becomes the king that everything must fit. *Igulim* are the dream and the passion, *teshuva*; *yosher* is the practical, the good deeds, where the bottom line is whether you do it.

phrases.he: וכשבא הרצון לעצמו הזה להיות בפועל ממש
phrases.en: and when this *ratzon* for Himself comes, that He actually wants to do it
it's the opposite

blocks.title: Dreaming of a home
blocks.text:
**And when this ratzon for Himself comes, that He actually wants to do it**, it is the opposite. First there is the *ratzon* that is just his taste, and he is thinking about a particular thing. Say the guy wants a home: "Oh, I'd really like to have my own space." He starts picturing, dreaming about his dream house, how he would like it to be, what he thinks is cool, and he makes a whole picture. He even starts looking at particular houses, but he is not actually thinking of doing it. He is thinking of doing it, but it is not really thinking of doing it; it is all kind of dreaming, he is not serious.

Then there comes a point where he decides he is actually going to do it. When he has figured out clearly enough what he wants, he decides to do it, and his whole perspective changes. Once he decides on a particular thing that he is actually going to do, he has to stop dreaming and start doing it.

His focus becomes the opposite. Until now his focus was on what he wants, so everything always had to be transparent, to remember that the main thing is what he wants and that he can choose anything; like they tell kids, "You can be whatever you want to be." It became a particular *ratzon*, but when you actually want to do it, you have to change your focus. In *igulim*, the biggest thing, the one that surrounds and defines everything, is what you want.

blocks.title: The Frierdiker Rebbe's plan on the boat
blocks.text: There is a story of the Frierdiker Rebbe (the Previous Rebbe). When he was coming to America, on the boat he told his secretary to take out paper, and he dictated his plan for America: that he wanted to make *Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch*, *Kehos* and *Machane Israel*. Why do it here? Why not wait until he got to America, evaluate the situation, and then make the plan? He said, "Because I don't want to come there and already be influenced by what I see, and then my plan will be an American Judaism. I want to have a European Judaism, an uncompromised ideal of the way things should be."

So there are always two steps. First you have to make a goal, and when you decide on your goal you should not consider the outside world. Decide, in theory, if everything could go just as you dream, what would your dream be? What is your ideal? There the top priority, the top circle, has to be what you want: what would really make you happy? Everything else has to be flexible to that, transparent to it.

blocks.title: I need a million dollars? I'll get a job
blocks.text: Then, when you decide you are actually going to do it, you have already picked a certain thing based on this dream. Now you put that down, and that goal becomes your top priority; everything has to fit within it. You have to figure out how to get it to be like that, and that is not compromisable: it has to look exactly like that. "Well, that's going to be hard." "I don't care if it's going to be hard. What do I have to do to do it?" "It's going to cost you a lot of money, take a lot of time." "I don't care, I'm going to do it. What do I have to do? I need a million dollars? Okay, I'll get a job then." Or I'll take out a loan, or ask my parents, whatever it is. You figure out how to do it.

So when you are going to do it *b'poel mamash*, everything is defined the opposite way. You make the *sof maaseh* the top thing, the king of everything; it is totally not flexible, and it defines everything else. That is the difference between *igulim* and *yosher*. When you actually want to do it, that is *yosher*, the ten *sefiros* of *yosher*, and there the *maaseh* (deed) becomes the top.

blocks.title: Getting the pizza
blocks.text: "What are you in the mood to do tonight?" Your main consideration is what you would really like to do, if everything went perfectly; you don't think about whether there is a way to do it. In theory, you would like to go get pizza. So you decide, "Okay, that's it, I'm going to do it," a firm commitment that you are going to figure out a way to get the pizza. Then you start figuring it out: first I need to get dressed, find my clothes; then I need wheels, a way to get there; then money: where am I going to get the cash? You start scraping around for cash. Finally you find a way to get there and pay for it. Or if that doesn't work, you can make it yourself. If you really want to do it, you will figure out a way. *Ein davar ha'omed bifnei haratzon*: nothing stands in the way of the will.

It is the same thing. First G-d was thinking that He wants to make the *dira b'tachtonim*, and He was planning it out in *igulim*, so everything was transparent to this *ratzon*, to reveal the thing He wants. Once He figured out a certain form, a certain *maaseh*, and decided that He wants it to come out *b'poel mamash*, that becomes the top thing, and everything that happens in the *hishtalshelus* from then on is going to be according to that *sof maaseh*. That becomes the *Keser*. The *Malchus* of the higher one becomes the *Keser* of the lower one: it becomes the king. Everything has to fit with that *ratzon*. If the king tells you, "I want you to move this mountain," you cannot tell him no; you have to figure out a way to do it. And it is going to happen.

blocks.question: Is this the change from igulim to yosher, or from yosher to igulim?
blocks.text: No. You go either from *igulim* to *yosher* or from *yosher* to *igulim*, either way, but here we are talking about going from *igulim* to *yosher*. You just finished the ten *sefiros* of *igulim*, and now the *Malchus* of *igulim* is becoming the top thing, totally set.

But in a way it is not just the ordinary *Malchus* of the higher one becoming the *Keser* of the lower one; it is a little different, because it is not the same *Malchus*. Since your main *ratzon* now is that it should actually happen, you still have to figure out exactly how and what it is going to look like. You just decided you are going to make a home like this, but you still have to figure out what the house is going to look like. Your focus is still on the physical building; you do not care so much about the planning and the *ratzon* for it. The *ratzon* for the house is only there to get the house, to motivate you to actually get it, because you do not really care about wanting the house; you want the home.

There are two *ratzonos*. The *ratzon* of *yosher* is the lowest thing; you do not care about it. The *ratzon* of *igulim* is the highest, the main thing you care about: that you should get the pleasure you want. The pleasure you will get from getting the physical building is just something you create as a low means to an end, to get you to make the house. It is like a candy, a bait.

Whether you enjoy finding a house, house shopping, is the thing you care about least. And you see that people usually do not enjoy house shopping very much, because it is the flimsiest *ratzon* and *taanug*. You create the *ratzon* to go house shopping only enough to motivate you to do it; as soon as you have enough motivation, you do not care about it anymore. Your intellect is a little bigger, because you need it to make it in the right way; the *middos* are more important, that you should feel good about it; and the main thing you care about is that you should actually have the house.

So we just finished the *sefiros* of *igulim*, where the top one is the main one and the inside one is the least important. Why? Because there you are focusing on what you want. Whatever you use to represent what you want is just a token representation; it does not really reach the thing it represents, so you see it as transparent and kind of irrelevant. Say you are making a language and have to pick a name for something: the name is really irrelevant, you can pick any name, because the main thing is you, what you decide. You see that whatever you decide, that is what it will be called.

blocks.text:
The same now, as we come to Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur. The whole purpose of Elul, Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur is to recognize the *sefiros* of *igulim* until we get to the top *igul*. We want to have *mesirus nefesh* for G-d Himself, the *Baal HaRatzon* (the One whose will it is), and realize that everything is whatever He wants. If He told us to chop wood, we would chop wood; if He tells us to jump off the roof, we'll jump off the roof; if He tells us to run around waving our hands and screaming like an insane person, we'll do that. Whatever G-d wants to happen in the world is what happens. If He wants there to be eleven *sefiros*, there will be eleven *sefiros*. All these things, nature and order, the *dira b'tachtonim* and the *gilui Atzmus*, are all invented by Him, and really irrelevant.

So to do *teshuva* (return) you have to say, "I don't care about Shabbos, I don't care about *aveira* (sin), I don't care about Torah and *mitzvos* at all, I don't care about anything; just whatever G-d wants me to do. If He tells me to do that, I'll do it." You do not care about it as a thing on its own that essentially has something to it. "And this whole *dira b'tachtonim* thing, we don't care about that either." That is *teshuva*: to reconnect to the original source, which here is the first *igul*.

blocks.text: From Yom Kippur to Sukkos is going into *yosher*, and in the *sefiros* of *yosher* it is the opposite. Once you make that commitment, that whatever G-d wants you will do and everything else is irrelevant, then once G-d picks something He wants you to do, that thing takes on the full force of your *mesirus nefesh*. If G-d tells you to put on *tefillin* every day, you will die to put on *tefillin* every day, and nothing is going to stop you. Communist Russia could not stop them from putting on *tefillin* every day or keeping Shabbos, even down to tying your shoelaces: if somebody tells you to tie your shoelaces the way the *goyim* tie their shoelaces, "you'll laugh in their face and let them kill you." So even for the smallest *prat* of the *ratzon* you will have total *mesirus nefesh*.

blocks.text: But to get to this next step you first have to stop caring about the things themselves; they have to be irrelevant to you. That is the *igulim*, where you realize that the main thing is just His *ratzon*. Then, when it comes to *b'poel mamash*, when G-d chooses the way He wants it to be, it switches to *yosher*, and the main thing becomes the *maaseh*: it has to be like this, according to the outward side, the *pratim* of *halacha*. You do not care about the *kavanos* (intentions); they are irrelevant, just ways to get you to that thing. The main thing is not your *kavana* and your feelings and "all that holy stuff"; the main thing is that you do it. Whatever you have to do to get yourself to do it is fine, but it has to be done exactly like this, and that becomes the top thing. When it comes to *b'poel mamash*, the *maaseh* becomes the main thing.

blocks.text: Like the story told last week about the Frierdiker Rebbe coming to America, and the *shliach* (emissary) going to Johannesburg, "I think." When you sit down in 770, or on the boat to America, and make your plan, that is *igulim*: you make the plan based on what you want, without considering what is possible and practical; everything else is *batel* (nullified) to that. Once you choose one plan *b'poel mamash*, that is your goal, and now you have to figure out how to get it. It becomes totally set, and everything you do is just to figure out how to get there, and even how to get yourself to want to do it. That is a *hachlata* (a decision): once you decide this is how it is going to be *b'poel mamash*, you switch, and the main thing becomes the *maaseh*.

blocks.title: A kid in a toy store with a dollar
blocks.text: There is a point in planning, say which house you want, where you are flexible: it could be this one, it could be that one. That is for a certain stage. Eventually you have to make a decision: "That's it. I'm going to do only one." You have to pick one and only one, and it is hard for people to make that jump; "it's an immaturity." You ever see kids going into a bakery or a toy store with only a dollar? They could buy anything, but they want all of it, so whatever they finally get is disappointing, because it is only this thing and not everything else. But you have to pick one thing, decide that is it, and not change your goal. Every time you change your goal, you start over. You decide, make a firm resolution to do it no matter what, and everything has to be just to figure out a way to do it. That is how you do things.

blocks.text:
That is why on Sukkos you go into the *sukka*: to realize that the *mitzvos* are only like a temporary structure. You have to be able to see through, and realize that you are doing them only because G-d said so: to see the *makif* of the *igulim* in the *yosher*. That is why it has to be temporary, and why you have to see through the roof.

"So I like to tell people on Sukkos that the purpose of Sukkos is to teach us that you're not supposed to be *frum* (religious)." People get a certain picture of what it means to be *frum*, and that becomes their goal; they want to be like that and forget that they just want to do whatever G-d wants. But you have to go out of your box. The whole year you have a house, a set structure, like a *Shulchan Aruch*, your picture of how you are supposed to be, and you try to keep everything within that box and protect it from outside influences. But every now and then you have to do *teshuva*, remember why you are doing it, and remember that it is temporary, a flexible thing. Once you realize that, you have to make it set again; most of the year it has to be a house.

blocks.text: But you have to at least start off with the *kavana* that you are doing it *lishma* (for its own sake). That is why in *halacha* the main thing is always that when you start doing something you have to remember that it is *lishma*: when you start, that is when you decide to do it, and you have to decide to do it because G-d said so. Once you decide to do it, you can forget why; the main thing is that you do it. Now it is a different *ratzon*: you decided you are going to do it, so you focus on how to do it. You do not have to hold the *kavana* the whole time, as long as that was the consideration when you initially decided to do it.

blocks.text: **The ratzon becomes hidden, and it goes into sechel.** Now you say, "Okay, that's it, I want to actually get a house." You take the *ratzon* and put it aside: now the main thing is not my *ratzon* anymore but the *sechel*. The *sechel* has to tell me what is a reasonable thing to want.

blocks.title: Buckingham Palace for the garage
blocks.text: In *igulim* you say, "Yeah, I think I would like to live in a great big palace, maybe Buckingham Palace, or maybe we'll use Buckingham Palace for the garage and build a bigger palace." Then he comes to actually do it, reaches into his pocket and sees he has two nickels and a dime; for that he could buy a cardboard box and live outside the museum. So his intellect tells him that he will either have to drop his expectations a little, or get a job, or come up with some more reasonable thing, and also figure out a way to do it.

Even if he does not lower his desire, in a way he does, because he has to make a practical picture of what he wants. In the *sechel* the picture becomes something limited, and he also has to figure out a practical way to do it. The thing of the *oros d'Tohu* (lights of Chaos) and the *kelim d'Tikun* (vessels of Repair) is that you do not lower your final goal, but you figure out a practical way that will start leading you toward it. Normally, though, people do not do *oros d'Tohu* with *kelim d'Tikun*; they just do the *oros d'Tikun* and the *kelim d'Tikun*. We are not up to *Tikun* yet, but for now it is almost the same thing.

So the *sechel* becomes the main thing: **and the sechel surrounds the ratzon, meaning that it's bigger than the ratzon**, and the *ratzon* does not really reach the *sechel*. What you want is very nice, but if it does not make sense, that's too bad. The *sechel* is more real now than the *ratzon*. The *sechel* gets to tell the *ratzon* what it should want; the *sechel* can change the *ratzon*, but the *ratzon* cannot change the *sechel*. The *sechel* is on top.

**Then the sechel gets hidden and gets put into the middos, one under the other.** It sounds very good on paper, in theory, but then the *middos* kick in and tell the *sechel* which plan you are going to do: "Okay, I know that in theory I could do that, but I'm sorry, I'm scared, I'm not going to do it." Or, "I don't like doing it." There are certain things you just are not willing to do. "You can make a lot of money being a garbage man, it has good benefits." "Yeah, I don't want to do that." So the *sechel* then has to go into the *middos*.

blocks.question: Are the middos the same ratzon?
blocks.text: No, it is not that *ratzon*. *Middos* means the way you relate to something, the way you react. There is a *ratzon* that is higher than *sechel*, and there is a *ratzon* that is lower than *sechel*; the *ratzon* lower than *sechel* is in the *middos*.

blocks.title: I like candy
blocks.text: Take a small example: I like candy. That is my *ratzon*, the one higher than *sechel*. Your *sechel* tells you what will get you candy and what will not: if you behave, you get candy. Then the *middos* mean the way you are going to react. Say your parents are watching you, and you have a choice to listen or not to listen: how are you going to react? Once you plug the *ratzon* into the *sechel*, *ratzon* plus *sechel* equals *midda*. It is automatic, a function: put a certain *ratzon* into the *sechel*, and the *sechel* spins out which *midda* you should have. That you now look at listening to your parents as a good thing and have a *chesed* toward it, and are scared to go against them because then they won't give you the candy: those are *middos*, the way you are going to react to the situations. Your inner desire is for the candy.

Before, the *sechel* was the bigger circle and the *middos* the smaller circles inside. Now the *sechel* is *metzamtzem* (contracted), and the *middos* go around it; then the *middos* are *metzamtzem*, and the *maaseh* goes around them. That is where we are up to now: one under the other, **until the sof maaseh goes on top of everything, the highest one of everything.**

These are two separate *hishtalshelus*'s that happen simultaneously, the *igulim* and the *yosher*. First there are the *igulim*, a circle inside a circle, all the way down to the *sof maaseh*. At the same time, though it starts after it, come the *sefiros* of *yosher*, which look like a person in three lines. The point of the person in three lines is that the top one is *metzamtzem* and *mislabesh* in the lower one, and it keeps going down: as you go down, the higher ones keep going into the lower ones. They do not just stay where they are.

blocks.title: A swimming pool
blocks.text: In *yosher*, first you want to figure out what you want, which is like *Atzilus*. Then what that means: if you like to swim, that means a swimming pool. Then exactly what form you want it in, how big and what to build it out of, which is like *Yetzira*. Then how to build such a thing, which is like *Asiya*. In *igulim*, as you go down, of course you also want all that, but the lower you go, the less you care about it, because it is not your main *ratzon*. That is why people like to daydream: the circles keep getting smaller and farther from the real thing.

No, in *igulim* the final thing is just a daydream; it is all a daydream in *igulim*. When you get to the final thing and imagine building the house, that is the most fake. The most real thing is that you want it, and the final thing, imagining yourself digging out the swimming pool, is the most fake, because it is so far from you actually doing it. But when you finish imagining it and say, "Okay, I want to actually do it," then you can start actually wanting to do it, and first you figure out what you want.

blocks.title: A swimming pool
blocks.text: Let's say you just say, "Oh, I'd like to swim, I like to be able to swim," and that becomes *mislabesh* in the *ratzon* for a swimming pool, and that's it. Now you do not want to swim anymore; you want a swimming pool. The *ratzon* to swim you could get with a lake, or the beach, but you decided no: you do not want to live at the ocean or near a lake, you want to live in the city and have a swimming pool. Once you decide that, the other *ratzonos* get totally hidden and covered over. All you see is that you want a swimming pool, and hidden inside it is the kernel of truth, that you do not really want the swimming pool, you want to be able to swim. That kernel of truth is the *igul* of *ratzon*, now *metzamtzem* into the *sechel*.

blocks.title: A swimming pool
blocks.text: Then, with the *ratzon* for a swimming pool, you look through catalogs of swimming pools and see one you think is good for your price range, your house and your size. Now those *middos* (and *middos* also means dimensions: how big, what it is made of, the price, all the specifications) become the main thing. The general picture in your head, that you want a swimming pool, becomes *metzamtzem* and *mislabesh* in those *middos*: you want that one. "Yeah, that's what catalogs do." They get you to go from wanting a pool to wanting this pool.

"I see this happen all the time with people." A second ago they were not sure what they wanted; anything that would do the job. They're hungry: "I don't know what I want, I'm in the mood for anything." Then all of a sudden their heart is set on one thing, "Okay, I want it," they get all excited, and they forget why they wanted it. Now if it turns out not so practical, a real pain to get, they cannot just drop it and get something more practical. "No, I wanted it. Oh, what can I do? Is there some way I can get it?" It becomes a big crisis that they cannot get it the exact way they envisioned, and changing the way they are going to get it is not an option. It is a little bit of an *akshanus*, a little stubborn.

Then wanting that specific thing becomes *mislabesh* in a certain *maaseh*. Say they decide to work to save up money: now they want to work to get the money, and they can get so caught up in the working that they forget why they were doing it. That is one of the things with *ratzonos*: there is no real *hishtalshelus* in *ratzon*, and especially in the *igulim* a lower *igul* can blow up and become a bigger *igul*. As you go down the *hishtalshelus*, once you associate a higher stage with a lower one, the lower stage takes over and becomes everything, the all-encompassing goal, and everything else becomes hidden in the background.

blocks.question: Why does yosher look like a person?
blocks.text: First of all, there is a *yosher* that does not look like a person yet, necessarily. But it is the way a person works: the *ratzon* goes into the *sechel*, the *sechel* into the *middos*, the *middos* into the *maaseh*, and then it comes out. When you want to actually do something, these are the steps you do it through, and since the *ratzon* is going through those steps, it is called going through a human process, the shape of a person. The *igulim* are like the soul before it comes into the body, and *yosher* is like the soul going into the body: when the soul goes into the body, it has to work through the form of the way people work, so it goes in that shape.

In the *igulim* you still go through all the steps, but in the lower steps the *ratzon* stays on top. It does not become *mislabesh* inside them, which means the *ratzon* is never going to become *batel* to the *sechel*; the *sechel* is *batel* to the *ratzon*. The *ratzon* bribes the *sechel*: you want it, and you will figure out a reasoning to fit it; you are biased. Then your *sechel* bribes the *middos* to come up with the *midda* that is the best approximation of the *sechel*, and the *middos* bribe the *maaseh* to figure out what you will do. So you tell yourself you will do these crazy things to accomplish the *middos* you want.

*Yosher* is the opposite. *Igulim* are a passion-oriented kind of thing; in *yosher* your main orientation is the practical, and finally the main thing becomes what the best way is to do it. That becomes the top thing, and everything else fits with it. The *maaseh* becomes the context that defines everything: if it is most practical to do it a certain way, you change the *middos*, you change the exact form of what you wanted to fit what is most practical, and that changes the *sechel* and the *ratzon* and everything. Because your main goal is to actually do it, everything has to fit with what is practical to actually do. That is what it means to be practical.

This is *teshuva* and *maasim tovim* (good deeds): *teshuva* is *igulim*, and *maasim tovim* is *yosher*. These are the two steps, *ratzo* and *shov* (running and returning), *MaH* and *BaN*, which really include everything: the *igulim* are *MaH*, and the *yosher* is *BaN*.

inside of the *poel mamash* was *machshava*
and inside that is the *middos*

phrases.he: ובמדות מלובש החכמה ובינה ובחכמה מלובש הרצון והתענוג
ונמצא פנימי מכולם הוא הרצון והתענוג,

this is *yosher*

phrases.he: כשבא בבחינת התלבשות העליון בתחתון כו'
phrases.en: when the upper one goes into the lower one

blocks.text:
**The final thing, the maaseh b'poel mamash**, includes everything: **inside of the poel mamash was machshava, and inside that is the middos**, and in the *middos* *chachma* and *bina*, and in the *chachma* the *ratzon* and the *taanug*.

So now **the most inner, hidden thing is the taanug and the ratzon, and the most external thing, the lowest thing, is the maaseh.** The *maaseh* has now become the top thing, on top of everything, the most outside thing: it is what you see. In *yosher*, what you see most on the outside is the *maaseh*, whereas in *igulim* the main thing you see is the *ratzon* and the *taanug*, and you see the *maaseh* as just a representation of it.

This is also a difference. Is the main thing the thought, or is the main thing the deed? "The thought that counts" is the motto of *igulim*: the main thing is what you wanted, you had good intentions. In *yosher* they say, "Yeah, well, the path to hell is paved with good intentions, my friend." The main thing is the bottom line: "Show me the bottom line. Did you do it or not?" *Maaseh hu ha'ikar* (the deed is the main thing): "I don't care about all your good intentions. Show me the buckaroos." The Frierdiker Rebbe says you need cold, hard cash: you have to make *kove'a itim l'Torah* (set times for Torah) and actually do things. Cold, hard cash. That is *yosher*.

In *yosher* the main thing is, which is actually this week's *parsha*, the whole point of this week's *parsha*: G-d wants you to do *yosher*; that is what He said. You do not have to worry about the *igulim*. *Hanistaros la'Hashem Elokeinu v'haniglos lanu ul'vaneinu*: the hidden things are the *igulim*, and they are G-d's business. Why He wants you to do it and what He is going to get out of it, that is all His business. Your business is what He told you: do this, and if you do this, this will happen. That is why it says, *ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od, b'ficha uvilvavcha la'asoso*. G-d told you clearly, black on white, in the Torah what He wants you to do, and the main thing is the *mitzvos*, that you actually do them. Do not worry about all the spiritual levels; the bottom line is you have to do it. And it is very easy to know whether you did it.

If you look in the Torah itself, it only tells you the bottom line, what it wants. The Oral Torah and the Rabbis tell you what you need to do to get yourself to do it. For example, the Torah says you are not supposed to have all these different bad relations, so the Rabbis tell you that therefore you have to dress and act in a way of *tznius* (modesty). The Torah does not tell you all those details, because that is not the main *ratzon*; it is just how to get yourself to do it. The bottom line is that whatever you have to do to get yourself to do it, that is your business. "I'm paying you to finish the job. You're the expert, you figure out how to do the job, but I want it to look like this. Whatever you got to do to make it look like that, do it." The Rabbis, the Oral Torah, tell you what you have to do to do it, the behind-the-scenes stuff, but the bottom line is whether you do it.

So that is *yosher*. That is why it says *Elokim asa es ha'adam yashar*, G-d made man in a way of *yosher*, straight, *v'heima bikshu tachbulos*, and they started making schemes in *igulim*. They started saying, "It's true that G-d told us to do this, but I look into the *igulim* and I see that what He really wants is this, and really it doesn't have to be this way; He could want it that way. So maybe I'll do it this way, and it'll be even better, and He'll like it even better." They think into what He really wants and try to make a scheme to do better than what He told them.

Which in a way we are going to do, by the way: that is the *inyan* of *teshuva*. *Teshuva* is doing something better that G-d did not even ask us to do; but that is also a source of sin, because we are not listening to Him.

**This is yosher, when the upper one goes into the lower one.**

sections.title: The ratzon kadum goes by circles, and comes from the reshimu through a short line
sections.summary: Because the *ratzon kadum* is still for oneself, it goes by way of circles, its first circle the general *makif* of all the worlds. Before it, the beginning of the *Kav* is a short line, one little point that carries the essence and stands for all of it, as a hair comes from the brain; so from the *reshimu*, still infinite though limited, the *Kav* measures out one little *ratzon kadum*.

it's still within yourself
